note.explanation: An element’s relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the masses of its isotopes, using their percentage abundances.
examples: For krypton, the relative atomic mass is 83.7.
For chlorine, the relative atomic mass of the light isotope is 34.95.
note.simple: Multiply each isotope’s mass by its percentage abundance, add the results, then divide by 100.
note.checkQuestion: Lead has isotopes ²⁰⁴Pb, ²⁰⁶Pb, ²⁰⁷Pb and ²⁰⁸Pb with abundances 2%, 24%, 22% and 52%. What is its relative atomic mass?
note.title: Calculating Relative Atomic Mass
steps: Multiply each isotope mass by its percentage abundance.

options: The mass of an atom compared with one-twelfth the mass of carbon-12
The number of protons and neutrons in an atom
The mass of an atom in kilograms
The number of isotopes in an element
mcqs.stem: What does relative atomic mass compare?
rationales: This is the definition given in your textbook, using one-twelfth the mass of carbon-12 as the reference.
The number of protons and neutrons is the mass number, not relative atomic mass.
Relative atomic mass is a comparison on a scale, not a mass in kilograms.
The number of isotopes does not define relative atomic mass.

options: 1/12 the mass of an atom of carbon-12
The mass of one atom of hydrogen-1
mcqs.stem: How is one atomic mass unit (amu) defined?
rationales: An amu is defined as one-twelfth the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
Hydrogen-1 has a mass of about 1.007 amu; it is not the definition of an amu.
The mass of a proton is not the reference definition used here.
The mass of a neutron is not the reference definition used here.

options: Divide each isotope mass by its abundance and add
Multiply each isotope mass by its percentage abundance, add the products, and divide by 100
Add the isotope masses and divide by the number of isotopes
mcqs.stem: Which method calculates relative atomic mass from isotope masses and percentage abundances?
rationales: Dividing the masses by abundance does not give the weighted-average formula.
This follows the formula in your textbook for percentage abundances.
A simple mean ignores the different abundances of the isotopes.
Multiplying all isotope masses is not the calculation method.

mcqs.stem: An element has isotopes of mass 20 and 30 with abundances 50% each. What is its relative atomic mass?
rationales: 20 is only the mass of the first isotope, not the weighted average.
The weighted average is (20 × 50 + 30 × 50) / 100 = 25.
30 is only the mass of the second isotope, not the weighted average.
35 is greater than the mass of either isotope, so it cannot be their average.

mcqs.stem: An element has isotopes of mass 40 and 42 with abundances 75% and 25%. What is its relative atomic mass?
rationales: 40 is the mass of the more abundant isotope, but the other isotope also affects the average.
The calculation is (40 × 75 + 42 × 25) / 100 = 40.5.
41 would be the average if both isotopes had equal abundance.
42 is only the mass of the less abundant isotope.

mcqs.stem: An element has two isotopes. If one isotope has an abundance of 72%, what is the abundance of the other isotope?
rationales: 18% does not make the two abundances total 100%.
The abundances must total 100%, so the other abundance is 100 − 72 = 28%.
72% is the abundance already given, not the other isotope’s abundance.
82% would make the total abundance 154%.

explain.title: Why relative atomic mass is useful
explain.body: Atoms of different elements have different masses. A common reference scale lets us compare them and helps us work out the ratios in which reactants combine.

explain.title: The reference unit
explain.body: The relative atomic masses of elements are expressed in atomic mass unit (amu). It is defined as one-twelfth the mass of an atom of carbon-12. One amu is 1.67377 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

explain.title: Isotope abundances make a weighted average
explain.body: An element can have several isotopes, and each isotope has its own natural abundance. The relative atomic mass is calculated by multiplying each relative isotopic mass by its abundance, adding the products, and dividing by 100.

explain.title: Finding an unknown isotope mass
explain.body: If the overall relative atomic mass and isotope abundances are known, put the unknown isotope mass in the formula. Set the expression equal to the given relative atomic mass and solve the equation.

mistakes: Do not use a simple average of isotope masses; their abundances are usually different.
Do not pair an isotope mass with the wrong abundance.
Do not forget to divide by 100 when using percentage abundances.
When solving for an unknown isotope mass, show the equation and each rearrangement step.
